episodes.text: Failed the entrance exam for the elite Ecole Normale Superieure despite prior preparation; rather than abandoning the goal, moved to Paris, enrolled elsewhere, won a top-physics-student prize, and retook the exam, passing with a high rank.

Painstakingly and manually hand-separated mirror-image forms of tartrate crystals under a microscope based on tiny asymmetric facets, founding the field of stereochemistry -- a discovery built from unusually careful, repetitive manual observation rather than a single flash of insight.

Advanced and publicly defended the minority scientific position that living microorganisms, not spontaneous chemical decomposition, caused fermentation, directly contradicting the dominant contemporary scientific view.

In the spontaneous-generation dispute with Pouchet, delivered a rhetorically confident public Sorbonne lecture ("a mere chimera") that later historical assessment calls "brilliant but hardly objective" -- and the Academie's deciding commission was staffed by his own friends and defenders, not a neutral panel.

Both Pasteur and rival Pouchet were working from the same false shared assumption (neither knew heat-resistant bacterial endospores existed); Pasteur argued from confident public rhetoric rather than acknowledging the method's real limitations, even though his conclusion happened to be correct.

As director of scientific studies at the Ecole Normale Superieure (1858-67), ran student discipline in an inflexible, authoritarian manner, dealing "summarily and unsympathetically" with complaints, and was "openly appalled" by student insubordination.

Mandated a disliked mutton stew be served and eaten weekly and threatened expulsion over smoking; when the large majority of roughly 80 students resigned rather than comply, did not back down -- ultimately cost him the ENS administrator post in 1867.

At direct government request, devoted five full years (1865-70) to investigating a silkworm disease, a field in which he had essentially no prior background -- historians describe this as an "epistemological rupture" that converted him from a chemist into a biologist.

Early in the silkworm-disease investigation believed the visible "corpuscles" he observed were symptoms rather than the cause of the disease; revised this view as more evidence came in rather than defending the initial hypothesis past its useful life.

Three of his five children died of typhoid fever within his lifetime (ages 2, 9, and 12); accumulated grief and overwork from this period is directly linked by multiple sources to a 1868 stroke that permanently paralyzed part of his left arm and leg.

Despite the stroke's partial paralysis, continued working, relying much more heavily from that point on trusted assistants (Roux, Chamberland) to carry out the physical/manual laboratory work he himself directed.

After France's defeat in the Franco-Prussian War, vowed to inscribe all subsequent scientific works with "Hatred toward Prussia. Revenge! Revenge!"; returned an honorary German M.D. in protest, publishing the angry exchange as a pamphlet; declined a Prussian honor even near the end of his life in 1895.
Turned down job offers from Milan and Pisa after the war to remain in France, reportedly reasoning that leaving in the wake of France's defeat would amount to desertion.

Discovered vaccine attenuation essentially by accident when unused cholera cultures left exposed during a vacation period weakened and produced immunity rather than disease when injected -- productively noticed and capitalized on an unplanned experimental outcome rather than discarding it.

In the anthrax-vaccine priority dispute, contested and downplayed veterinarian Toussaint's earlier immunization approach "on grounds of jealousy" per the historical record, while claiming public credit through his own large-scale public demonstration.

At the public Pouilly-le-Fort anthrax-vaccine trial (1881), deliberately built his chief public skeptic -- a veterinarian who rejected germ theory -- into the trial's own oversight structure, letting him select the animals and supervise the final exposure; addressed the large public crowd of politicians, journalists, and farmers in "a lay and familiar tone" and reportedly "charmed his audience."

The vaccine actually used in the public Pouilly-le-Fort trial was not his own publicly-implied method (which had not reliably worked) but a chemically-inactivated preparation originated by rival Toussaint and refined by his own assistant; Pasteur ordered the substitution kept quiet and never publicly disclosed it -- discovered only when his private notebooks were published nearly a century later.

Despite the concealed substitution, when honored with the Legion of Honor for the anthrax success, insisted his assistants Roux and Chamberland also be honored -- taking the higher grade himself but ensuring they received formal recognition rather than accepting sole individual credit.

In the 1881 dispute with rival bacteriologist Robert Koch -- whose colleagues publicly denounced Pasteur's anthrax research and questioned his methodological rigor -- replied dismissively in his own subsequent speeches rather than disengaging or conceding methodological points.

Carried a separate, long-running lifelong priority dispute with chemist Antoine Bechamp over credit for core fermentation and germ findings -- a third, distinct multi-decade priority conflict beyond Toussaint and Koch.

Facing a child (Joseph Meister) considered near-certain to die of rabies without intervention, personally decided -- despite holding no medical license, a real legal/professional risk -- to administer his experimental, previously only animal-tested rabies treatment; his own documented words describe the decision as made "not without acute and harrowing anxiety."

Did not make the Meister decision alone or immediately -- his own most trusted collaborator, Roux, initially refused to participate, considering it premature and unjust since the treatment had only been tested in animals; a second physician ultimately persuaded him to proceed and administered the injections himself, since Pasteur held no medical license.

Public claims about how extensively the rabies method had been validated in animals before treating Meister did not match his own private notebooks -- claimed roughly 50 successful prior animal trials publicly while notebooks document about 11, and at least two other human patients besides Meister reportedly received the treatment with worse, undisclosed outcomes around this period.

As institute director, invited immunologist Metchnikoff -- who held his own differing, competing theory of immune response -- to join and develop his ideas at the institute rather than treating him as competition to exclude; his senior collaborator Roux is documented as someone who "did not always agree with" Pasteur, not merely an obedient subordinate.

Instructed his family that his private laboratory notebooks should never be shown to anyone and did not permit assistants to keep independent notes of their own, maintaining a personal monopoly over the documented research record throughout his career; the notebooks stayed sealed within the family until 1964.

Explicitly framed the new Institut Pasteur's mission in humanitarian, universalist terms rather than nationalist ones ("You don't ask someone who is suffering, 'What country are you from?'") -- a notable contrast to his own well-documented personal wartime nationalism.
